science.title: The science of procrastination
science.lead: Procrastination isn't about time or character. It's a way of coping with unpleasant emotions through avoidance.
science.c1_d: Laziness is not wanting to act. Procrastination is wanting to act — and choosing something easier instead. The difference is emotional, not motivational.
science.c2_d: The limbic system demands relief now; the prefrontal cortex plans ahead. As stress rises, the limbic system wins — and the video replaces the report.
science.c3_d: Our brains discount future rewards. A deadline 'tomorrow' feels infinitely lighter than today's discomfort — hence the eternal Monday promises.

types.title: Four types of procrastinators
types.lead: Different types need different fixes — so it helps to know which one is yours.
types.t1_d: 'If it can't be perfect, it can't be started.' Delay protects against the risk of an imperfect result.
types.t2_d: The task triggers fear of failure or judgement. Avoidance kills the anxiety instantly — and reinforces the habit.
types.t3_d: The task is too big and fuzzy to start. The brain, sensibly, chooses not to choose.
types.t4_d: 'I do my best work under pressure.' Last-minute adrenaline becomes both fuel and excuse.

quiz.title: What type of procrastinator are you?
quiz.lead: Three questions, two minutes, zero diagnoses. Just a starting point.
quiz.q1: When do you procrastinate the most?
q1_opts: When I'm afraid the result won't be good enough
When I fear being judged for the outcome
When the task is huge and I don't know where to start
When it's boring and the drive only shows up at the deadline
quiz.q2: How do you feel when you open your to-do list?
q2_opts: The urge to redo everything perfectly
Anxiety and an urge to close the tab
Freeze: I don't even know what to grab first
Boredom, until the deadline starts breathing down my neck
quiz.q3: What usually 'saves' you at the last moment?
q3_opts: Endless revisions up to the last second
Talking it through with someone, then doing it
Frantically breaking the task into tiny steps

perfectionist.name: Perfectionist
perfectionist.text: What slows you down isn't laziness, it's the bar. A working strategy: 'the first draft is allowed to be bad' — deliberately make version one rough.
perfectionist.cta: Turning 'rough first version in 10 minutes' into a habit is easier than it sounds.

anxious.name: Anxious Avoider
anxious.text: Procrastination is your painkiller. What helps isn't 'pulling yourself together' but lowering the stakes: do so little that the anxiety doesn't kick in.
anxious.cta: Gentle nudges and tiny steps lower anxiety better than promises to yourself.

overloader.name: Overloaded
overloader.text: The problem isn't discipline, it's fuzzy tasks. Turn 'write the report' into 'open the doc and write one paragraph'.
overloader.cta: Good news: breaking tasks down is a skill that's easy to automate.

thrill.name: Thrill-Seeker
thrill.text: You love deadlines as a catalyst. The trick is to give yourself intermediate deadlines — several small sprints instead of one giant leap.
thrill.cta: Personal deadlines and light tracking turn 'the final night' into a series of manageable sprints.

methods.title: Techniques that actually work
methods.lead: Four evidence-based tricks with a zero learning curve.
methods.m1_d: 25 minutes of work, 5 of rest. It works because starting is cheap: anyone can endure 25 minutes.
methods.m2_d: Shrink the task to a two-minute step. 'Write an article' becomes 'open the file and write the headline'.
methods.m3_d: The formula 'after X, I will do Y'. Research shows a concrete when-where link roughly doubles the odds of starting.
methods.m4_d: Not 'do the project', but 'write one list item'. The brain resists the size of the work, not the work itself.

facts.title: Curious facts
facts.lead: Procrastination is as old as writing — and it has quite a biography.
facts.f1_d: While writing The Hunchback of Notre-Dame, Hugo famously had his servants hide his clothes so he couldn't leave the house — the novel met its publisher's deadline.
facts.f2_d: The Hitchhiker's Guide author missed deadlines so regularly that editors literally locked him in hotel rooms until the book was done.
facts.f3_t: A word with a built-in excuse
facts.f3_d: 'Procrastination' comes from Latin pro (forward) and crastinus (of tomorrow) — literally 'belonging to tomorrow'.

faq.title: FAQ
faq.a1: No. Laziness is an absence of desire; procrastination is avoidance despite desire. Different mechanisms, different solutions.
faq.a2: No, it's not a diagnosis. But chronic procrastination often goes with anxiety and ADHD — in that case, it's worth discussing with a professional.
faq.q3: Which technique should I start with today?
faq.a3: The two-minute rule: pick one task and shrink it to a two-minute step. Starting is the most expensive part.
faq.a4: Tools don't replace the decision to start, but they lower friction: ready-made templates, task breakdown and gentle reminders remove the 'where do I begin' barrier.
